The surah opens with a question that draws attention to al-Ghashiya, the Resurrection that overwhelms people with its terrors, as most commentators explain; Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak say it is one of the names of the Last Day. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b say it is the Fire that covers the faces of the disbelievers. Al-Tabari holds that the verse includes both meanings, since both are overwhelming coverings. In either case, faces on that day are humbled and weary; they burn in a fierce fire, drink from a spring whose heat has reached its extreme, and have no food but the dari', which neither nourishes nor satisfies.

The commentators agree that humiliation, fatigue and toil describe the people of the Fire, but they differ on when these states occur. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say the labour takes place in the Fire, in dragging chains and shackles; 'Ikrima and al-Suddi say it refers to acts of disobedience in this world, followed by suffering in the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab wept on seeing a Christian monk and took the verse as a warning to those who strive sincerely in error. As for the dari', most lexicographers and exegetes identify it as dried shibraq, a thorny plant; others say it is zaqqum, stones, or a tree of fire, and Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan suggest reconciling these views by recalling that the Fire has different levels.

Many authors note that the interrogative form is meant to arouse attention and wonder. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir point out that the contrast between the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise shows that the surah presents both groups together.

This verse describes the faces of disbelievers on the Day of Judgment as "humbled" (khashi'a), meaning abased and disgraced. The commentators explain that "faces" stands for the persons themselves, since humiliation and sorrow show on the face. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take this humiliation to occur in the Hereafter, while others hold that it applies also in worldly life. On the phrase "toiling, exhausted" (amila nasiba), most explain it as weariness and hardship: al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr say they drag chains and shackles in the Fire and sink into it as camels sink into mud, while ʿIkrima and al-Suddi relate it to evil deeds done in this life followed by suffering in the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas and Zayd ibn Aslam apply it to monks and worshippers who went astray, whose labour brought them no benefit; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wept when he heard this verse before a Christian monk. Al-Razi and Ibn ʿAtiyya offer further readings, all centred on suffering and fatigue. Ibn ʿAshur notes that these three descriptions also carry a warning to those who were not humble before God in worldly life.

This verse describes the faces of the damned on the Day of Resurrection as humbled, and as toiling in exhausting labour, such as dragging chains and collars and wading through the Fire. The commentators differ on when this toil takes place. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr say it happens in the Fire, where they labour and suffer as punishment. 'Ikrima and al-Suddi say it refers to deeds done in this world in disobedience, followed by weariness in the Hereafter. Zayd ibn Aslam explains that their works, done without guidance, bring them nothing but fatigue, and their end is the Fire. Another view, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Zayd ibn Aslam, holds that the verse refers to monks and hermits among the People of the Book. According to accounts cited by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab wept on seeing a monk and recited this verse. All agree that the verse concerns the damned, that the word 'faces' stands for the persons themselves, and that 'toil' means weariness and hardship. On the reading, Ibn Kathir reports a transmission with the accusative 'nasiba', which expresses censure or a state, while most readers use the nominative. Ibn 'Ashur sees the three descriptions as a warning to the wretched who neglected humility before God, righteous action and effort in this world, so that their recompense is humiliation, hardship and exhaustion.

This verse describes the fate of the faces of those who disbelieve on the Day of Judgment: they will enter a scorching fire and be given drink from a spring that has reached the extreme of its heat. The commentators explain that "taslā" means to be exposed to the fire's heat and endure its burning, and that "ḥāmiya" means the fire has been kindled and heated for a very long time, so that no heat equals it. Ibn Abbas adds that it has been heated and rages against God's enemies. Most agree that "faces" stands for their owners, and that this punishment is the requital for their disbelief or sins.

The differences concern first the recitation. The Kufans and others read "تَصْلَى" with a fatha on the tā', while Abu Amr, Abu Bakr and others read "تُصْلَى" with a damma. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct in meaning. The exegetes also differ on "āniya": Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it to mean water that has reached the limit of its heat, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean present or ready.

As for food, it is the ḍarīʿ. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima identify it as the shibraq, a thorny plant; Said ibn Jubayr says it is stones; Ibn Zayd says it is a thorn of fire; and al-Hasan says it is zaqqum. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi reconcile these views by holding that the damned occupy different levels of hell, so some eat zaqqum, others ghislin, and others ḍarīʿ.

This verse describes the drink of the people of the Fire: they are given to drink from a spring whose heat has reached its utmost limit. Most commentators follow this meaning. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that 'aniyah' means its heat has reached its end, and they report that a single drop of it would melt the mountains of the world, citing the verse about a boiling, piercing liquid. Ibn Zayd reads the word as 'present' or 'ready', a view that most scholars did not adopt. Qatada and al-Hasan say the fire has been kindled over this spring since creation, and that its people are driven to it parched with thirst. Al-Razi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that this water scalds the faces and cuts the bowels, which they relate to the verse 'they are given boiling water that cuts their intestines'. The point on which these views meet is that this drink is scalding, does not quench thirst, and only causes torment. On recitation, Abu Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read 'tuqa' with a damma, in parallel with 'tusla', while al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the pronoun refers to the persons concerned and not only to the faces.

This verse in Surat al-Ghashiya describes the food of the people of the Fire in the Hereafter. The commentators explain that they will have no food except dari', a thorny plant that the Quraysh called al-Shibraq while it is green and dari' once it dries out. It is described as a deadly poison that animals avoid. The Qur'an adds that it neither fattens nor relieves hunger, so the food itself becomes a further punishment. The scholars agree that it is among the most foul and repugnant foods. They differ on its precise nature. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ikrima identify it as dried shibraq, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report and Ibn Zayd describe a tree or thorn of fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it is stones, al-Hasan connects it with zaqqum, and others mention a valley in Hell or ghislin. Abu Hanifa and several lexicographers describe it as a bad pasture that does not fatten livestock, citing verses by Abu Dhu'ayb and al-Hudhali. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi reconcile it with the verse in al-Haqqa by explaining that Hell has several levels, each with its own food. Some report that the polytheists claimed their camels grew fat on dari', and the verse refutes this, since animals avoid it once dry.

This verse describes the food of the people of the Fire: it neither fattens nor relieves hunger. The commentators agree that al-Ḍarīʿ is a thorny plant, called al-Shibraq while green and al-Ḍarīʿ once dry; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that camels eat it only when fresh, and Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it is a thorny plant of the Fire, with a saying attributed to the Prophet describing it as a thorn in the Fire. Al-Baghawi reports that the polytheists claimed their camels grew fat on it, but they were lying, since camels eat it only when moist. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur note that Ḍarīʿ may refer to zaqqum or ghislin, the different punishments of the Fire explaining the different foods. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi explain that the verse negates the two benefits of food, satisfying hunger and giving strength or fat. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say Ḍarīʿ is a stone or a part of the hidden punishment, while Ibn Kaysan holds it is a food that makes its eaters beg and humble themselves before God, and Ibn Ashur adds that the verse is meant to make their torment more humiliating.

This verse describes the faces of the believers on the Day of Judgment as radiant and joyful. Ibn Kathir explains that the blessing of comfort becomes visible on them, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand it as brightness and beauty, or as being immersed in luxury. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, this state is the reward for their striving in this world. It stands in direct contrast with the humbled and exhausted faces of the damned described just before. The commentators agree that the word 'faces' refers to the people themselves. They also agree on the meaning of being 'pleased with their striving': al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it as contentment with their deeds in this life, while others see it as contentment with the reward they receive. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the 'high' garden may refer to its elevation above the Fire or to its loftiness in rank. Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di emphasise the richness of the blessings described next, including raised couches, cups, cushions and carpets. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse deliberately contrasts with what precedes it. The commentaries do not draw any legal rulings from this verse, which is limited to describing the state of those who are blessed.

This verse describes the faces of the believers on the Day of Resurrection as radiant and content with what they achieved in this life. The commentators explain that their contentment comes from seeing the reward. Al-Tabari takes it to mean that they are pleased with the deed they did in the world, or with the reward of their striving in the hereafter. Ibn Kathir reports that Sufyan understood it as their being pleased with their own work. Al-Razi offers two readings, one in which they praise their conduct for the good end it has brought them, and another in which they are content with the reward they witness; he prefers the second. Ibn 'Ashur understands the contentment as praise for what they did in obeying God. Al-Mawardi and others note that the verse contrasts these faces with the humbled, weary faces in the fire.

The commentators agree that these people will dwell in a lofty garden, high in place or in rank. They differ on the meaning of the phrase la laghiya, usually rendered as idle talk. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it as lies or sin, Mujahid as insult, al-Kalbi as oaths, and Ibn Juzayy as blameworthy speech. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' explain that only wise words and praise of God are heard there, and al-Razi likewise holds that the garden is free of all vain speech.

The exegetes then describe the flowing spring, the raised couches, the cups set in place, the aligned cushions and the spread carpets. They agree on these objects but differ on their sense: some say the couches are raised in rank, others in height, and Ibn Kathir notes that the carpets are spread here and there for those who wish to sit on them.

This verse describes the bliss of the people of Paradise, who are in an elevated garden. The commentators understand the word elevated in two ways: as height of place, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress, or as height of rank, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi mention, while Abu Hayyan and others combine both meanings. It stands in contrast with the humbled faces in the Fire, since these faces are radiant and content with the reward of their striving in this world. The exegetes agree that no vain speech is heard there, though they differ on what the word lagha covers. Ibn Abbas takes it as falsehood, Mujahid as abuse, Qatada as sin, and al-Kalbi as oaths, while al-Farra' holds that the people of Paradise speak only in wisdom and praise of God. They also mention the flowing spring, the raised couches, the cups set in place, the aligned cushions and the spread carpets. Al-Mawardi records several readings and meanings of the phrase raised couches, and some note that the verses on the camels that follow are a sign of God's power. Many scholars link this passage with the reference to camels that comes next, as a lesson for the listeners.

This verse, within the description of the people of Paradise, states that they will hear no idle or vain speech there. The apparent meaning the commentators give is that no hurtful word will reach them, and that their own speech is wisdom and praise of God for the lasting blessings He has granted them. All agree that lagha means vain talk, but they differ on its form: Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean lying, Mujahid insult, Qatada falsehood and sin, al-Hasan disobedience, and al-Kalbi oaths, while al-Farra' in one view made it a general rule covering every idle word. Al-Razi notes that Paradise is a place of earnestness and truth, free of frivolity. On the reading, Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it in the passive, while the rest read it with the active verb and a fatha; al-Tabari holds that all these readings are sound in meaning. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that the passage answered the polytheists who mocked the idea of Paradise, and God invited them to reflect on the creation of camels, which most commentators take to mean the camel itself, though al-Mubarrad understood clouds. The commentators also describe the flowing springs, the raised couches, the cups set in place, the aligned cushions and the spread carpets, and they discuss whether 'raised' means physically high or of high rank, and whether 'spread' means laid out or scattered.

This passage of Surat al-Ghashiya describes the bliss of the people of Paradise. The commentators explain that in the lofty Garden there is a flowing spring, meaning many springs whose waters run without the need for a channel dug for them, a point on which the exegetes broadly agree. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi take the word 'spring' as a collective noun covering many springs, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a quality that completes the Garden's beauty. The verses go on to mention raised couches, cups placed within reach, aligned cushions and spread carpets. Opinions differ on the meaning of 'raised': al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand real elevation, Ibn Kathir stresses great height, and al-Baghawi reports that the couches lower themselves for whoever wishes to sit. As for the zarabi, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir call them rugs, while al-Farra' describes them as fine-piled hangings. After this description the surah turns to the camel, a animal well known to the Arabs, to invite reflection on God's creation. This verse therefore paints the splendour God prepares for believers and calls the reader to contemplate His power.

This verse describes the thrones of the people of Paradise, called sururun marfu'a, raised thrones. The commentators agree that the word means lofty and elevated. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, said their frames are of gold set with chrysolite, pearls and rubies, and that they stay raised until their owner comes, then lower themselves to receive him before rising again. Al-Tabari adds that a believer, seated on them, sees all the kingdom and blessings his Lord has granted him. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the height may be physical, in the thing's size, or in its rank. Al-Razi reports that the word may also mean that they are exalted in the eyes of their people because of their dignity, a view also given by al-Farra. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take the height as literal, while Ibn 'Ashur sees the phrase as a description of the beauty of the palace furnishings. Some reciters and commentators read the word differently, but the common understanding is elevated. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy note the further sense of exalted rank. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that these blessings differ in reality from what exists in this world, even though their names are the same.

This passage of Surat al-Ghashiya describes the bliss of the people of Paradise and mentions 'cups set in place'. The commentators explain that the akwab are cups or vessels without handles, spouts or lips, and that 'set in place' means they are ready and arranged before them, or placed at the edges of the flowing springs, so that they drink whenever they wish. Al-Tabari says they stand at the edge of the spring and that whenever they want to drink they find them full of drink. Ibn Kathir adds that they are prepared and waiting for whoever wants them among their owners. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that this furniture is arranged so that no one needs to prepare it, which expresses ease and abundance. Ibn Ashur sees in the phrase an image of the lasting pleasure of drink, which is never taken away from their hands. The meaning of 'set in place' is thus debated. Al-Razi also records, without adopting it, the view that the cups are of intermediate size, between small and large, as in another verse; Abu Hayyan finds this unlikely. The commentators agree that the nearby items, the raised couches, the cushions and the rugs belong to the same picture of comfort. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note that readings differ on a neighbouring word, without changing the general sense of the description.

This passage of surah al-Ghashiya describes the delights of the people of Paradise on that day: their faces are radiant and content with the deeds they did in the world. The commentators explain that the namariq are cushions arranged side by side, so that a person sitting anywhere can lean on one. They are mentioned together with the zarabi, which are precious rugs and carpets spread through the gatherings. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Kalbi define them as cushions, supports or seats, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also accept the sense of cushions.

The commentators agree that this picture is meant to convey comfort and abundance prepared for the blessed, with many carefully arranged seats and furnishings. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that placing them in rows expresses plenty and complete preparation. Ibn 'Ashur adds that such items belong to the furnishings of fine homes, so the verse brings the unseen closer to what people know of luxury.

The differences concern the meaning of the words. Some grammarians report the form nimriqa with a kasra, which al-Farra' mentions. Ibn Qutayba takes mabthuta to mean scattered through the gatherings, whereas Qatada and Ikrima take it as spread out or piled one upon another. Al-Alusi regards the zarabi as the finest rugs, while al-Raghib traces the word to striped cloths later used for carpets.

Finally, Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di stress that these blessings share names with things in this world but differ in reality, which no one can fully know, citing the verse that no soul knows what is hidden for them of joy for the eyes.

This verse describes the furnishings that God has prepared for the people of Paradise, namely zarabi, which the commentators understand as broad, luxurious carpets with a fine nap. For the word mabthuthatun, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abbas and Qatada explain it as spread out or laid flat, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Ikrima took it as piled one upon another, while al-Farra' took it to mean numerous and Ibn Qutayba to mean scattered through the gatherings. Al-Qurtubi prefers the sense of many and scattered, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya list the same meanings. Most commentators link the verse to the preceding ones on the raised couches, the cups set in place and the cushions arranged in rows, all of which belong to one picture of luxury. Al-Baghawi notes that the unbelievers mocked these descriptions, which is why the verses on camels follow. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith on the rivers and palaces of Paradise, though the commentators treat the details differently. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn 'Abbas remind readers that the names are familiar from this world while the realities are beyond it. All agree that the verse promises a comfort that exceeds what people know in this life.

In this verse God invites those who deny the resurrection to reflect on His creation as evidence of His power, beginning with the camel: the wonder of its making, its strength, its docility toward humans despite its great size, the many benefits it provides such as riding, carrying loads, milk and meat, and its endurance of thirst. The commentators explain that the camel is mentioned because the Arabs lived by it and knew it better than any other animal, and some report that the unbelievers mocked the description of Paradise, so they were reminded of God's handiwork. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur understand the camel in its ordinary sense, whereas al-Mubarrad takes al-ibl to mean the clouds, a view that al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi consider unsupported. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the grouping of four things, camel, sky, mountains and earth, is natural for a desert Arab who sees them all around him on his travels. The commentators say the mountains are firmly set and the earth is spread out, and Ibn Sa'di notes that this spreading does not contradict its roundness. God then tells His Prophet to remind people, since he has no authority to compel them; whoever turns away and disbelieves will receive the greatest punishment, and all will return to God, who will call them to account. The exegetes differ on the exception 'except one who turns away': some hold it to be connected to the preceding command, others take it as disconnected, and some consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword.

In these verses God calls on those who deny the resurrection to reflect on His creation, which shows His power. He asks them to look at the camels, how they were created: remarkable animals that carry heavy loads, endure thirst and let themselves be led by a child. He asks them to look at the sky, how it was raised, at the mountains, how they were set firm, and at the earth, how it was spread out. According to the commentators, the mention of camels answers the wonder of the unbelievers at the description of Paradise, and camels were among the most valued possessions of the Arabs. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take al-Ibil to mean camels. Al-Mubarrad, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and others understand clouds, which al-Zamakhshari reads as a figurative comparison. On the meaning of raised, some say it means raised far off without pillars, others that nothing can reach it. On spread out, most say it means made level and smooth, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di note that this does not contradict the earth's roundness. Afterwards the Prophet is commanded to remind without compelling. Al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas take musaytir to mean one who dominates, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean one who forces faith. Abu Dawud holds the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Tabari does not. The punishment of the one who turns away and disbelieves is, for most, the Fire of Hell. The commentators thus agree that the passage calls for reflection on God's signs as a basis for belief in resurrection and judgment.

God invites those who deny the Resurrection to reflect on His creatures, which display His power: the camel, created and made subservient to people; the sky raised without visible pillars; the mountains firmly set so the earth does not shake; and the earth spread out and made smooth. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, agree that these signs are offered as evidence that God can resurrect and recompense. They explain that the camel is singled out because it was the most valued property of the Arabs and the animal they saw most often. Al-Razi lists its many uses: milk, meat, riding, carrying loads, endurance of thirst, and obedience even to a small child. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir note that the mountains anchor the earth and keep it from swaying, and Ibn al-Qayyim adds their benefits in water, minerals, shelter and protection from winds. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take the word 'spread out' to mean flattened and made level, while Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur observe that this does not contradict the earth being spherical. The recitations differ: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali read the verbs in the first person, and al-Hasan reads the last with a doubled consonant. Al-Mubarrad suggested that 'the camels' here means clouds, a view most exegetes reject. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'laba, who relied on these same signs. The common message is that reflecting on these creations leads to belief in God's power and in the Resurrection, and that the Prophet's role is to remind, not to compel.

This verse calls attention to the camel, how it was created, to the sky, how it was raised, to the mountains, how they were set firm, and to the earth, how it was spread out and levelled. The commentators explain that this looking means reflection and drawing lessons from the signs of God's power, and that these creatures show God's ability to resurrect and to requite, something the deniers cannot refuse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baghawi note that camels were among the most valued possessions of the Arabs, which explains why they are mentioned first, and that their pairing with sky, mountains and earth matches what the desert Arabs constantly saw. There is general agreement that the earth was spread for living upon, that the mountains anchor it, and that the sky was raised without pillars. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that for some scholars the spreading does not rule out that the earth is spherical, while Ibn Atiyya holds that the apparent sense is that the earth is a flat surface and that scholars of the law do not affirm its roundness. As for the meaning of al-Ibil, al-Mubarrad, Abu Amr ibn al-Ala and al-Sam'ani take it to mean clouds, a view several regard as isolated, while the majority understand the familiar camels. The commentators conclude that the Prophet is only to remind, not to compel; that whoever turns away and disbelieves will suffer the greatest punishment; and that the return and the reckoning belong to God.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to keep reminding and admonishing people, for his duty is only to convey and remind, not to dominate them or force them to believe. Commentators explain 'musaytir' as one who holds dominion or a tyrant: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say so, while Ibn Zayd reads it as the prohibition against forcing people into faith. Regarding the exception 'except whoever turns away and disbelieves', al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it as a disjunctive exception ('but whoever turns away'), whose punishment is the 'greatest torment', understood by most as Hell. Al-Mawardi also mentions the view that it means eternal abiding in the Fire, and al-Baghawi notes that these people were already punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity. On whether the verse was abrogated by the verses of fighting, Qatada and Ibn Zayd held that it was, while al-Zarkashi, as cited by al-Baghawi, rejected this, arguing that a command to gentleness is not abrogated merely by a later command to fight. All agree that the return of mankind and their reckoning belong to God alone.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to continue reminding and admonishing people, for his only duty is to convey the message, and he has not been sent to compel them to believe. The commentators agree that « musaytir » means one who holds dominion over others or forces them. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain the phrase as a denial of compulsion, while al-Hasan takes it to mean « lord » and al-Dahhak « one who dominates ». As for the exception in « except he who turns away and disbelieves », most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, read it as a disjunctive exception meaning « but », and they identify « the greatest punishment » as the Hellfire, although some, such as al-Tha'alibi, mention killing and captivity in this world as well. On abrogation, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Baghawi, and many others, held that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Zarkashi, quoted by al-Baghawi, considered that view weak and argued that the command of leniency was bound to a particular situation. Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi note the possibility of a connected exception, meaning that the Prophet has authority over those who turn away and disbelieve by means of jihad. All agree that the return and the reckoning belong to God alone.

This verse, read with the one before it, tells the Prophet ﷺ that he is charged with reminding people, not with forcing them to believe, and that whoever turns away from the truth and persists in disbelief is left to God. Commentators differ on how to read the exception in 'except whoever turns away and disbelieves'. Most take it as a disjunctive exception, meaning 'but whoever turns away and disbelieves'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Uthaymin hold this view. Ibn Kathir explains that turning away means abandoning the acts of worship, and disbelief means rejecting the truth in heart and tongue. Ibn Ashur holds that this reading implies no abrogation.

Others read the exception as connected to the preceding command: remind everyone except the one who turns away and disbelieves, or you have authority only over those who turn away and disbelieve. Al-Tabari, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report both readings. Al-Suddi says the reminder is not addressed to such a person, and al-Hasan says this came before the command to fight. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi mention that many scholars saw the verse as abrogated by the verses on fighting. Ibn Abbas and Qatada read the opening word as a particle of attention, and Ibn Masud's reading changes the sentence structure.

On the greatest punishment, most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin, identify it as Hell. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the unbelievers were also punished in this world through hunger, captivity and death, and al-Razi lists these views without deciding between them. Al-Qurtubi reports that Ali had an apostate executed on the basis of this verse.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to continue reminding and admonishing people. He is not sent to compel them to faith; his task is only to convey the message. The verse then makes an exception for the one who turns away and persists in disbelief: God will punish him with the greatest punishment, which the commentators agree is the Hellfire in the Hereafter. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, take the exception as disjunctive, meaning that whoever turns away after being reminded will be punished. Others, such as Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu al-Su'ud and the authors of the Jalalayn, read it as a continuous exception, meaning that the Prophet has authority over the one who obstinately refuses, or that reminding should continue except for those whose hope of faith has been lost. Al-Nahhas and al-Razi, followed by others, hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, whereas Ibn Ashur and Ibn Uthaymin regard it as unabrogated, since it denies that the Prophet has any compulsory power. On recitation, some read the opening word as a particle of alerting and others vary the letter of "bi-musaytir" between sin, sad and fath. As to the greatest punishment, some identify it with the torment of the Hereafter, while others link it to the hardships of this world such as hunger, death and captivity. The verse ends by affirming that all will return to God and that He will call them to account.

The commentators explain that the verse means that all creatures return to God alone, and that their reckoning and recompense rest with Him alone. It comes in Surat al-Ghashiya, which orders the Prophet ﷺ to remind people and denies him any power to compel them; the verse reassures him that the matter of accountability belongs to God. The commentators agree that "iyab" means return, namely the return to God after death and resurrection, and that "His reckoning" means the requital of their deeds, whether good or evil.

Al-Tabari, Qatada and Mujahid report that the reckoning belongs to God; Ibn Kathir sees in the verse a consolation for the Prophet and a statement that recompense is God's responsibility. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the fronting of the adverbial phrase and the particle "thumma" intensify the warning: the return is only to the Almighty who punishes, and only He holds them to account. Al-Razi adds that God must avenge the wronged, otherwise He would seem to approve of injustice, whether by His promise or by wisdom.

Readers differ over the form "iyabahum". The common reading is without doubling, whereas Abu Ja'far reads it with a shadda. Abu Hatim considered that reading impermissible, while others regarded the two as dialectal variants with the same meaning, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya offered morphological explanations for it.

As for the connection with the preceding verses, al-Zamakhshari sees it as a justification for not exercising compulsion over people, al-Razi as a consolation that eases the Prophet's sorrow over their disbelief, and Ibn 'Ashur as a reason why he is not required to force them to believe, with "thumma" marking a distance in rank.

The commentators explain that this verse, in the sūra al-Ghāshiya, reassures the Prophet ﷺ: all people will return to God, and their reckoning belongs to Him alone, so the Prophet's duty is only to remind. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others understand 'return' (iyab) as the coming back to God after death, and 'reckoning' (hisab) as the repayment for deeds, good or bad. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see in it a consolation that lifts from the Prophet the distress caused by his people's disbelief: the call is his, the account is God's.

The apparent meaning is broadly agreed: return and judgment belong to God alone. Al-Razi adds that the verse calms the Prophet's heart grieved by his people's rejection, and answers the objection that a right holder need not exercise it by saying that the reckoning is required by divine wisdom. Ibn 'Ashur reads 'inna' here as expressing emphasis and cause, and 'ala' as conveying the firmness of the reckoning, like a right God has imposed upon Himself. Al-Nasafi holds that 'ala' serves to strengthen the warning and does not mean an obligation, since nothing is owed to God.

On recitation, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan note that Abu Ja'far read 'iyyabahum' with a shadda; Abu Hatim rejected it as not permissible, while al-Zamakhshari considered it morphologically possible. As for 'illa' in the preceding verse, al-Qurtubi reports it is taken either as a connected or a disconnected exception, and some scholars regard the verse as abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir maintain that the reminder remains in force without abrogation.
